sections.heading: Devolution of power & finances to local levels

blocks.text: The **73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)** gave constitutional status to **rural (Panchayati Raj) and urban local bodies**, mandating **devolution of functions, funds and functionaries (3 Fs)** to enable grassroots self-government — though fiscal devolution remains weak.

rows: **Panchayati Raj**; added **Part IX & 11th Schedule (29 subjects)**; 3-tier system.
**Functions, Funds, Functionaries** — states must devolve; uneven in practice.
**SC/ST (proportional) & women (⅓, many states now ½)**; State Election Commission & State Finance Commission (Art. 243-I).

sections.heading: 🔎 Exam-ready deep coverage: devolution to local bodies

items: **73rd & 74th Amendments (1992)**: gave **constitutional status** to Panchayats (Part IX, **11th Schedule – 29 subjects**) & Municipalities (Part IXA, **12th Schedule – 18 subjects**); made local self-government the **3rd tier** of the federation.

**Mandatory features**: 3-tier PRIs (village–block–district) for states >20 lakh; **reservation** for SC/ST (population-proportion) & **1/3 (now often 50%) for women**; **State Election Commission** runs elections; **State Finance Commission (Art 243-I)** every 5 yrs recommends fiscal devolution; 5-year term; District Planning Committees.
**The '3 Fs' problem — Funds, Functions, Functionaries**: devolution remains uneven; heavy dependence on grants; weak own-revenue; parallel bodies dilute PRIs.
**AP**: strong PRI tradition; Gram Panchayat–Mandal Parishad–Zilla Parishad structure; **Mandal system** (introduced 1985, N.T. Rama Rao) replaced the old block/taluk for local administration.
73rd = rural (11th Schedule, 29 subjects); 74th = urban (12th Schedule, 18 subjects).
3 Fs; women's reservation ⅓ (½ in many states incl. AP); State Finance Commission.

prelimsPointers: **73rd Amendment (1992)** — Panchayati Raj; **Part IX & 11th Schedule (29 subjects)**.
**74th Amendment (1992)** — Municipalities; **Part IXA & 12th Schedule (18 subjects)**.
Three tiers of PRI — **Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti (block), Zilla Parishad (district)**.
**Gram Sabha** — the foundational body of direct village democracy.
Reservation — **SC/ST proportional; women one-third** (½ in many states including AP).
**State Election Commission** conducts local elections; **State Finance Commission** (every 5 yrs) recommends devolution.
Devolution of **3 Fs — Functions, Funds, Functionaries** remains uneven.
**73rd/74th Amendments (1992)** = constitutional status to Panchayats/Municipalities (Parts IX & IXA).
**11th Schedule (29 subjects)** = Panchayats; **12th Schedule (18 subjects)** = Municipalities.
**State Election Commission** conducts local polls; **State Finance Commission** (5-yrly) devolves funds.
'3 Fs' gap = **Funds, Functions, Functionaries**; AP uses the **Mandal** system (since 1985).
mainsAngles: Assess the devolution of powers and finances to local bodies since the 73rd/74th Amendments.

glossary.definition: The 1992 amendment giving constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions.
The assembly of all voters in a village, the base of Panchayati Raj democracy.
A body constituted every five years to recommend devolution of finances to local bodies.

blocks.text: **Constitutional bodies** are those **established directly by the Constitution**, giving them independence and permanence — the **Election Commission, UPSC, CAG, Finance Commission, Attorney-General** and others — the guardians of the democratic and financial system.

rows: **Art. 148**; audits govt accounts; 'guardian of the public purse'.
**Art. 280**; every 5 yrs; recommends Centre-State tax devolution.
**Art. 76**; chief legal adviser to the Union.
**Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (350B), National Commissions for SC (338)/ST (338A)**.
CEC + ECs; conducts national/state polls; removal like SC judge (CEC).
Recruitment to services; Chairman/members by President/Governor.
Every 5 yrs; centre-state fiscal devolution (15th FC — Chair N.K. Singh).
'Guardian of the public purse'; audits Union/State accounts; reports to PAC.
Chief law officer of Union / State.
Safeguard rights (NCBC got constitutional status via 102nd Amendment 2018).

items: Constitutional (in Constitution) vs statutory (by law): EC-324, UPSC-315, CAG-148, FC-280.
CAG = guardian of public purse; NCSC (338), NCST (338A) are constitutional.

prelimsPointers: **Election Commission — Article 324**; **UPSC — Article 315**; **CAG — Article 148**.
**Finance Commission — Article 280**; constituted every **5 years** by the President.
**Attorney-General of India — Article 76**; **Advocate-General of a State — Article 165**.
**CAG** — 'guardian of the public purse'; audits and reports to legislatures (via PAC).
**National Commissions for SCs (338) & STs (338A)** are constitutional bodies.
**Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities — Article 350B**.
Constitutional bodies derive authority **directly from the Constitution** (vs statutory bodies from law).
**Election Commission (Art 324)**; **UPSC (315)**; **Finance Commission (280)**; **CAG (148)**.
**CAG** = 'guardian of public purse'; audits reach the **Public Accounts Committee**.
**NCBC** got constitutional status via the **102nd Amendment (2018)** — Art 338B.
**GST Council = Art 279A**; **Attorney-General = Art 76**.
mainsAngles: Distinguish constitutional from statutory bodies with examples.

glossary.definition: A body established directly by the Constitution (e.g. EC, UPSC, CAG, Finance Commission).
The Comptroller and Auditor-General (Art. 148), auditor of government accounts.
A constitutional body (Art. 280) recommending Centre-State revenue sharing every five years.

blocks.text: **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)** are the **three-tier system of rural self-government** constitutionalised by the 73rd Amendment, tracing back to the **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957)**, and are the primary vehicle of **grassroots democracy and rural development**.

rows: Recommended the **3-tier PRI**; first launched in **Rajasthan (1959, Nagaur)** then Andhra Pradesh.
Recommended a **2-tier** system; PRIs as political institutions.
**Gram Panchayat → Panchayat Samiti (Mandal in AP) → Zilla Parishad**.
Extends Panchayati Raj to **Scheduled (tribal) areas** — Gram Sabha empowerment.
AP uses the **Mandal Praja Parishad** (mandal) as the middle tier.

sections.heading: 🔎 Exam-ready deep coverage: Panchayati Raj evolution

items: **Committees**: **Balwant Rai Mehta (1957)** — recommended **3-tier PRI** & 'democratic decentralisation'; **Ashok Mehta (1977)** — **2-tier** (Zilla + Mandal), political parties; **G.V.K. Rao (1985)** & **L.M. Singhvi (1986)** — constitutional status.
**73rd Amendment (1992)** implemented these — **Gram Sabha** as the foundation of direct democracy.
**PESA Act (1996)**: extends Panchayats to **Fifth Schedule (tribal) areas** — empowers the **Gram Sabha** over minor forest produce, land, water, disputes; key in AP's agency areas.
**Functions**: local development, welfare delivery (MGNREGA, PM Awas, water/sanitation), planning; **e-Panchayat**; Social Audit; issues — capacity, finances, elite capture.
Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) = 3-tier; Rajasthan first (1959), AP second; Ashok Mehta = 2-tier.
PESA (1996) extends PRI to Scheduled areas; AP uses Mandal tier.

prelimsPointers: **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957)** recommended the **three-tier Panchayati Raj**.

**Ashok Mehta Committee (1978)** recommended a **two-tier** system.
Three tiers — **Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti/Mandal, Zilla Parishad**.
**PESA Act (1996)** extends Panchayati Raj to **Fifth Schedule (tribal) areas**.
**Andhra Pradesh** uses the **Mandal Praja Parishad** as the intermediate tier.
PRIs deliver the **11th Schedule (29 subjects)** functions.
**Balwant Rai Mehta (1957)** = 3-tier PRI; **Ashok Mehta (1977)** = 2-tier; **L.M. Singhvi** → constitutional status.
**Gram Sabha** = foundation of Panchayati Raj; **PESA (1996)** empowers it in **Fifth Schedule** areas.
**73rd Amendment (1992)** gave PRIs constitutional status.
PRIs deliver **MGNREGA, PMAY-G, water & sanitation** at the grassroots.
mainsAngles: Trace the evolution of Panchayati Raj and its role in rural governance.

glossary.definition: The three-tier system of rural local self-government constitutionalised in 1992.
The 1957 committee that recommended the three-tier Panchayati Raj system.
The 1996 Act extending Panchayati Raj to Scheduled (tribal) areas with empowered Gram Sabhas.

blocks.text: **Governance** is the exercise of authority to manage a country's affairs; **good governance** adds **participation, transparency, accountability, rule of law and responsiveness**. **Public policy** is the government's course of action on public problems — increasingly delivered through **e-governance and citizen-centric reforms**.

rows: **Participatory, consensus-oriented, accountable, transparent, responsive, effective/efficient, equitable/inclusive, rule of law** (UN).
**RTI Act (2005), Citizen's Charters, Social Audit, e-governance**.
**G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E**; **DBT, Digital India, UMANG, CSCs**.

sections.heading: 🔎 Exam-ready deep coverage: public policy & governance basics

items: **Good governance (World Bank/2nd ARC)**: participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, accountability, equity, effectiveness, consensus.

**Transparency & accountability tools**: **RTI Act (2005)**, **Citizen's Charters**, **e-Governance (Digital India, DBT, UMANG)**, **Social Audit**, **Lokpal & Lokayuktas Act (2013)**, **Whistle Blowers Act, PIL**.
**2nd ARC (Veerappa Moily)** — landmark governance reforms (RTI, ethics, decentralisation, disaster management, e-gov).
**Policy cycle**: agenda-setting → formulation → adoption → implementation → evaluation; role of NITI Aayog, think-tanks, evidence-based policy.
**Citizen-centric governance**: Sevottam, grievance redress (CPGRAMS), minimum-government-maximum-governance.
Good governance = 8 UN attributes; RTI/Citizen's Charter/social audit = accountability tools.
e-governance: G2C/G2B/G2G/G2E; DBT & Digital India are flagship.

prelimsPointers: **Good governance** — 8 UN attributes (participatory, transparent, accountable, rule of law, responsive, equitable, effective, consensus-oriented).
**RTI Act (2005)** — empowers citizens to seek information; promotes transparency.
**Citizen's Charter** — a public commitment to service standards.
**Social audit** — public scrutiny of schemes (mandatory in MGNREGA).
**e-governance interactions — G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E**.
**Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), Digital India, Aadhaar, UMANG, Common Service Centres** — key initiatives.
**2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC)** made major governance recommendations.
**RTI Act (2005)**; **Lokpal & Lokayuktas Act (2013)**; **Citizen's Charter & Social Audit** = accountability tools.
**2nd ARC (Veerappa Moily)** = major governance-reform reports.

Good-governance pillars: transparency, accountability, participation, rule of law.
mainsAngles: Discuss the attributes of good governance and tools of accountability.

glossary.definition: Governance marked by transparency, accountability, participation, rule of law and responsiveness.

blocks.text: The **1991 Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation (LPG) reforms** transformed governance — shrinking the state's direct economic role and shifting it towards **regulation, facilitation and enabling** — spawning new **regulatory bodies** and a more **market-oriented, accountable** administrative style.

rows: State withdrew from production; rose as **regulator/facilitator** (SEBI, TRAI, CCI, etc.).
**SEBI (1992), TRAI (1997), IRDAI, CCI, PFRDA, RERA** — independent regulators.
Disinvestment, PPPs, ease-of-doing-business, single-window, digital services.
Greater transparency demands (RTI), citizen-as-consumer, service delivery focus.
**Regulatory capture, inequality, jobless growth, weakened public sector** concerns.

sections.heading: 🔎 Exam-ready deep coverage: LPG reforms & governance

items: **1991 LPG reforms** (Narasimha Rao–Manmohan Singh, BoP crisis): **Liberalisation** (end of licence-permit raj, delicensing), **Privatisation** (disinvestment of PSUs), **Globalisation** (trade/FDI opening, WTO 1995).

**Governance impact**: shift from **regulator/producer state → facilitator/regulator state**; rise of **independent regulators** (SEBI, TRAI, RBI's expanded role, CERC, IRDAI); PPP model; FDI-driven growth; but concerns — inequality, jobless growth, farm distress.
**Later reforms**: GST (2017), IBC (2016), FRBM, Ease of Doing Business, Make in India, disinvestment/monetisation.
**Federal angle**: states compete for investment (competitive federalism); cooperative institutions (GST Council, NITI Aayog).
LPG shifted the state from 'controller/producer' to 'regulator/facilitator'.
New regulators (SEBI, TRAI, CCI, RERA); PPPs, disinvestment, ease of doing business.

prelimsPointers: **LPG reforms (1991)** — **Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation** (under P.V. Narasimha Rao & Manmohan Singh).
Governance shifted from a **'controller/producer' to a 'regulator/facilitator'** state.
New **regulatory bodies** — **SEBI (1992), TRAI (1997), CCI, IRDAI, PFRDA, RERA**.
Growth of **Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs)** and **disinvestment**.
Emphasis on **ease of doing business, single-window clearances, minimum government-maximum governance**.
Concerns — **regulatory capture, rising inequality, jobless growth**.
The state increasingly acts as an **enabler and referee** of the market.
**LPG reforms 1991** (Narasimha Rao/Manmohan Singh) — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation.
Shift to a **facilitator/regulator state**; regulators = **SEBI, TRAI, IRDAI, CERC**.
Triggered by the **1991 Balance-of-Payments crisis**; WTO joined **1995**.
Later: **GST (2017), IBC (2016)**, disinvestment, Ease of Doing Business.
mainsAngles: Examine how the LPG reforms of 1991 reshaped governance in India.

glossary.definition: The 1991 Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation policy shift in the Indian economy.
An independent authority (e.g. SEBI, TRAI) overseeing a liberalised sector.
When a regulator serves the interests of the industry it regulates rather than the public.

blocks.text: Beyond constitutional bodies, governance relies on **statutory bodies (created by an Act of Parliament), regulatory bodies (overseeing sectors), and quasi-judicial bodies (tribunals/commissions with adjudicatory powers)** — the specialised machinery of the modern state.

rows: **NHRC, CIC, NCW, NGT, Lokpal, NITI Aayog (executive), UGC, SEBI** — created by law.
**SEBI (securities), RBI (banking), TRAI (telecom), IRDAI (insurance), CCI (competition), RERA (real estate)**.
**NGT, CAT, tribunals, NHRC, Lokpal, Election Commission (partly)** — adjudicate disputes.
Constitutional = in Constitution (EC, UPSC, CAG); statutory = by Act (NHRC, CIC).

sections.heading: 🔎 Exam-ready deep coverage: statutory, regulatory & quasi-judicial bodies

rows: Policy think-tank; cooperative federalism; no fund allocation.

items: **Constitutional vs statutory vs executive vs regulatory vs quasi-judicial** — a favourite distinction: e.g., **EC/UPSC/CAG = constitutional; NHRC/CIC/NGT/SEBI = statutory; NITI Aayog = executive**.
Statutory (by Act: NHRC, CIC, Lokpal) vs constitutional (EC, CAG) vs executive (NITI Aayog).
Quasi-judicial = adjudicatory (NGT, CAT, tribunals).

prelimsPointers: **Statutory bodies** are created by an **Act of Parliament** — **NHRC, CIC, NCW, NGT, Lokpal, UGC, SEBI**.
**Regulatory bodies** — **RBI, SEBI, TRAI, IRDAI, CCI, PFRDA, RERA**.
**Quasi-judicial bodies** exercise **adjudicatory** powers — **NGT, CAT (Central Administrative Tribunal), NHRC, tribunals**.
**NITI Aayog** is an **executive body** (resolution, 2015), not statutory.
**NHRC (1993)** — statutory; headed by a former CJI/SC judge.
**Lokpal (2013)** — anti-corruption ombudsman at the centre; **Lokayuktas** in states.
Constitutional bodies (EC, UPSC, CAG) differ from statutory ones in their **source of authority**.
**NHRC (1993), CIC (2005), NGT (2010), Lokpal (2013)** = statutory; **NITI Aayog (2015)** = executive.
**NGT** = environmental quasi-judicial body; **CAT/NCLT** = tribunals (Art 323A/B).
Regulators: **SEBI (markets), RBI (banking), TRAI (telecom), IRDAI (insurance)**.
**NHRC** is **recommendatory** (no binding power) — a common prelims point.
mainsAngles: Classify statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies with examples.

glossary.definition: A body created by an Act of Parliament (e.g. NHRC, CIC, Lokpal).
A body with powers to adjudicate disputes, like a tribunal (e.g. NGT, CAT).
An authority overseeing and regulating a specific sector (e.g. SEBI, TRAI).
